newsitem.title: FRANCE: France names two new members to central bank council.
newsitem.headline: France names two new members to central bank council.

text.p: The French government Friday named two new members to the Bank of France's key policy council in a move that could shift the balance of power at the independent central bank in favour of lower interest rates.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said Pierre Guillen, 69, former deputy head of the employers' federation CNPF, and Jean-Rene Bernard, 64, former deputy governor at property lender Credit Foncier, had been appointed to the nine-member monetary policy council.
He said there would be no change in policy and told reporters President Jacques Chirac had expressed confidence in the independent Bank of France to continue a stable and steady monetary policy.
But economists said the appointments could shift the bias in favour of slightly faster interest rate cuts.
Both men are seen as Chirac's personal choice, thereby increasing the government's leverage over the Bank of France, until now dominated by hawkish governor Jean-Claude Trichet.
Financial markets had been anticipating the decision for any sign of a softening in the bank's commitment to defending the stability of the franc against the mark.
The new members, viewed by economists as potentially more dovish on monetary policy, replace former journalist Jean Boissonnat and former banker Bruno de Maulde, whose mandates expire next week.
The two were seen as strong backers of the existing policy of maintaining French interest rates slightly above those in Germany to protect the franc's stability against the mark.
Asked by reporters whether the appointments indicated a shift in policy, Prime Minister Alain Juppe replied, "No, no, not at all. Rather the contrary."

Guillen, 69, said last month he was "radically against" devaluing the franc but, that "like many industrialists, I wanted interest rates to come down a little bit faster, but that's an opinion ... of a representative of industry."

Bernard, 64, is not thought to have any strong convictions on monetary policy. But he is close to Chirac and would be expected to follow the president's lead on policy, sources close to the selection process say.

The French franc weakened on the news, easing to 3.3772 per mark, down more than half a centime against its level late Thursday. Bonds showed little reaction to the appointments but stocks rose slightly on the hope of lower interest rates.

The appointment of the two new members is likely to create a new balance of power in the council, which until now had a six-to-three majority in favour of the existing cautious policy on interest rates, sources close to the bank say.
Guillen is seen likely to join ranks with members who have called publicly for faster rate cuts to boost growth and bring down unemployment, running at a record 12.7 percent.
Bernard, whose views on monetary policy are less well known, is likely to be the swing member in an otherwise four-to-four balance between doves and hawks on the council, analysts said.
